clinicalPearls: The classic presentation of cancer arising in the head of the pancreas is 'painless' jaundice; jaundice is visually detectable once bilirubin exceeds ~2 mg/dL and may be accompanied by pruritus from bile salt skin deposition (p.672).

Pain, when present, is typically mid-epigastric and 'boring' with radiation to the back (from retroperitoneal invasion of the splanchnic nerve plexus) and may be worsened by eating or lying flat (p.672).
A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in the setting of biliary obstruction is Courvoisier's sign (p.672).

Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and combined deep venous plus arterial thromboses (Trousseau's syndrome) can occur; metastatic disease is frequently associated with a hypercoagulable state requiring anticoagulation (p.672-674).

New-onset diabetes (especially with concomitant weight loss) or unexplained worsening of type 2/type 3c diabetes, or rising HbA1c/hyperglycemia in the preceding 1-2 years, may signal underlying pancreatic cancer (p.671-672).

CA19-9 is best drawn after the bilirubin has normalized because biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9; CA125 can help in the 8-15% of Lewis-antigen non-secretors who have undetectable CA19-9 (p.674).
Cigarette smoking is the greatest environmental risk factor, accounting for an estimated 25-30% of cases, with risk persisting at least 10 years after cessation (p.671).

Histologic/cytologic tissue diagnosis is essential and also enables molecular testing (next-generation sequencing for KRAS and other alterations) and microsatellite status determination, which increasingly guide therapy (p.674).
Signs of late-stage disease include a left supraclavicular Virchow's node and a periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule indicating peritoneal metastases (p.672-673).
harrison.pathophysiology: Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common and most lethal exocrine pancreatic neoplasm, characterized by infiltrating desmoplastic stromal reaction and arising in the head, body, or tail. Most cancers arise from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN, graded 1-3 in a progression model), with genetic alterations accumulating as PanIN grade increases; some arise from noninvasive cystic precursors (e.g., IPMN). The mutational landscape is dominated by four commonly altered genes: KRAS (mutated in 90-95%, primarily codon 12), p16/CDKN2A (inactivated in >90% of invasive tumors), TP53 (~75%), and DPC4/SMAD4 (~50%); BRCA2 is mutated in 3.5-10%. A 'KRAS wildtype' subset (more common in patients under 55) may harbor actionable BRAF mutations, oncogenic fusions (NRG-1, NTRK1-3), or microsatellite instability (p.672).
additionalDifferentials: Metastasis to the pancreas (renal, breast, lung, urothelial carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic pancreatitis (can be difficult to distinguish from adenocarcinoma and is itself a risk factor)
Metastatic disease to the pancreas from other primaries
additionalInvestigations: Dual-phase contrast-enhanced CT using a pancreas-cancer protocol (arterial and portal venous phases) to assess tumor-vessel relationships, resectability, and staging
Abdominal ultrasonography (often first imaging in the jaundiced patient)
18F-glucose PET to detect occult metastatic disease
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with EUS-guided core needle biopsy of pancreatic lesions
Tru-Cut core needle biopsy (preferred over fine-needle aspiration) for histologic diagnosis; percutaneous biopsy for liver/lymph node lesions
Next-generation sequencing for genomic alterations (including KRAS) and microsatellite status
Serum CA19-9 (drawn after bilirubin normalizes), CEA, and CA125
Staging laparoscopy (selectively, before or at definitive surgery)
redFlags: Painless obstructive jaundice (classic for head-of-pancreas tumor)
Palpable non-tender gallbladder with obstruction (Courvoisier's sign)
Unintentional weight loss with loss of muscle mass
New-onset diabetes, especially with concomitant weight loss
Mid-epigastric boring pain radiating to the back
Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis / venous or arterial thrombosis (Trousseau's syndrome)
Left supraclavicular Virchow's node or periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule (late disease)
harrison.prognosis: Pancreatic cancer is the most lethal human cancer, with an overall 5-year survival of about 13% (up from 3% in 1975). SEER estimates 5-year survival of ~44% for localized disease, ~16% for regional disease, and ~3.2% for metastatic disease. Late presentation is common, only about 10-20% of tumors are resectable, and the disease is the third leading cause of cancer mortality in the U.S. and projected to become the second by 2030 (p.671-672).
pitfalls: Drawing CA19-9 while bilirubin is elevated falsely raises the level, since biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9 (p.674).
8-15% of patients are Lewis-antigen non-secretors with undetectable CA19-9, so a normal CA19-9 does not exclude disease; CA125 may help in this group (p.674).
Even high-grade PanIN precursor lesions are not detectable by current imaging, limiting early detection (p.672).
For average-risk individuals with no predisposing factors there is currently no recommended screening (p.671).
Whether diabetes causes or is caused by pancreatic cancer is not clearly established (p.671).
Fine-needle aspiration cytology is acceptable but less preferred than core (Tru-Cut) biopsy, which yields adequate tissue for molecular testing (p.674).
Biliary stenting is not necessarily warranted if upfront surgery is planned, but is required (where medically indicated) before neoadjuvant systemic therapy (p.674).
harrison.severityClassification: Staged by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system (Table 88-2). Clinically also categorized by extent of disease and therapeutic approach (Table 88-3): resectable (~10-20%), borderline resectable/locally advanced, and metastatic (p.674).
